newsitem.title: USA: FTC issues rules to expedite anti-trust cases.
newsitem.headline: FTC issues rules to expedite anti-trust cases.

text.p: The Federal Trade Commission said Wednesday it was issuing new rules intended to speed up resolution of merger cases and anti-competitive or consumer fraud complaints filed by the agency.
An FTC statement said the changes included a new one-year deadline for administrative adjudications generally, and the establishment of a "fast track" option for merger cases.

Commissioner Mary L. Azcuenaga said the rules were a first step. "Some of the amendments seem clearly to be good ideas, and others may be worth a try to help expedite the commission's adjudicative proceedings," she said in a statement.

Under the changes, an FTC administrative judge must reach a decision within a year after the FTC files a complaint seeking to enforce various statutes, such as in anti-trust, anti-competitive or consumer fraud cases. Parties can still appeal an unfavorable decision to the full commission, and the appellate phase is not covered by the one-year deadline.

In addition, respondents in merger cases would have the option of placing the matter on a "fast track" for resolution by the commission within 13 months. This would be available to respondents in which a court has granted the FTC a preliminary injunction to block a deal while the agency pursues its challenge, the FTC said.

The FTC said the changes would be published in the Federal Register "shortly" and they would be effective upon publication. But it said that in any case beginning before January 1997 the FTC administrative law judge would be able to decide whether to apply the new rules or not.

The FTC statement said it was also seeking to make more information about these cases public. It said it would make publicly available the interlocutory orders issued by the FTC administrative judges and a quarterly status report on the progress of cases.
The reforms were made on the recommendations of a task force established by FTC Chairman Robert Pitofsky in May 1995, the FTC said. It said it was seeking public comment on them.
